'''''Convolvulus arvensis''''', or '''field bindweed''', is a species of [[Convolvulus|bindweed]] in the [[Convolvulaceae]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cullen |first=Elaine |title=Webb's An Irish Flora |date=2012 |publisher=Cork University Press |isbn=978-1-85918-478-3 |edition=8 |location=Cork}}</ref> native to [[Europe]] and [[Asia]]. It is a [[rhizomatous]] and climbing or creeping [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] with stems growing to {{Convert|0.5-2|m|ft}} in length. It is usually found at ground level with small white and pink flowers.

Other [[common name]]s, mostly obsolete, include '''lesser bindweed''', '''European bindweed''', '''withy wind''' (in [[basket willow]] crops), '''perennial morning glory''', '''small-flowered morning glory''', '''creeping Jenny''', and '''possession vine'''.

==Taxonomy==
Field bindweed was first [[Species description|described]] in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in the ''[[Species Plantarum]]''. In the following centuries, many [[subspecies]], [[variety (biology)|varieties]], and [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonymous taxa]] were discovered and described as purportedly new species in places including China, Russia, Egypt, and Morocco.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}} New species and forms were described as far as Chile, Mexico, and the state of California when botanists encountered the plant there,<ref name="WCSP">{{cite web |last=Govaerts |first=Rafaël |author-link=Rafaël Govaerts |date=2021 |title=''Convolvulus arvensis'' L., Sp. Pl.: 153 (1753) |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:265849-1 |access-date=9 July 2021 |website=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]]}}</ref><ref name=AFP>{{cite web |url=https://florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/Plant.aspx?id=1755 |title=''Convolvulus arvensis'' |last1=Wunderlin |first1=R. P. |last2=Hansen |first2=B. F. |last3=Franck |first3=A. R. |last4=Essig |first4=F. B. |date=8 July 2021 |website=Atlas of Florida Plants |publisher=Institute for Systematic Botany, University of South Florida, Tampa |access-date=9 July 2021}}</ref> although it is not native to these areas.<ref name=WCSP/>
[[File:Convolvulus Rosa 01.jpg|thumb|upright|''Convolvulus arvensis'', Zaamin National Park, Uzbekistan]]

In the ninth volume of [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]]'s ''[[Prodromus]]'', published in 1845, [[Jacques Denys Choisy]] reduced a number of these synonyms to ten varieties of ''Convolvulus arvensis'',<ref>{{cite book |last=Choisy |first=Jacques Denys |author-link=Jacques Denys Choisy |date=1845 |title=Prodromus systematis naturalis regni vegetabilis |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/55703981 |volume=9 |location=Paris |publisher=Fortin, Masson et sociorum |language=Latin |pages=406, 407 |doi=10.5962/bhl.title.286}}</ref> although he also recognised a number of species now also reduced to synonyms of ''C. arvensis''.<ref name=WCSP/><ref name=AFP/> Over time, most or all of these species and varieties were no longer recognised by the relevant authorities.<ref name=FOC>{{cite book |last1=Fang |first1=Ruizheng |last2=Staples |first2=George |date=1995 |chapter=''Convolvulus arvensis'' Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 1: 153. 1753 |chapter-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200018801 |title=Flora of China |url=http://www.efloras.org/volume_page.aspx?volume_id=2016&flora_id=2 |volume=16 (Gentianaceae through Boraginaceae) |location=St. Louis |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden Press |page= |isbn=}}</ref>

In the ''Flora of Great Britain and Ireland'' (2009), [[Peter Derek Sell]] described nine new [[Form (botany)|forms]] he believed he had discovered in [[Cambridgeshire]], along Fen Road in the village of [[Bassingbourn cum Kneesworth]]. The forms discovered in Bassingbourn cum Kneesworth were deemed not credible by subsequent [[Taxonomy (biology)#Author citation|taxonomic authorities]], however, and the species is currently considered to be [[Monotypic taxon|monotypic]] by most authorities.<ref name=WCSP/><ref name=AFP/>

==Description==
''Convolvulus arvensis'' is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] vine that typically climbs to {{Convert|1|m|ft}}. The vine produces woody [[rhizome]]s<ref name=FOC/> from which it resprouts in the spring, or when the aboveground vines are removed.

The [[leaf|leaves]] are spirally arranged, linear to arrowhead-shaped, {{Convert|2-5|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and alternate, with a {{Convert|1-3|cm|in|abbr=on}} petiole. The [[flower]]s are trumpet-shaped, {{Convert|1-2.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} diameter, white or pale pink, with five slightly darker pink radial stripes. Flowering occurs in mid summer<ref name="Clapham1968">{{Cite book |last=Clapham |first=A. R. |title=Excursion flora of the British Isles |last2=Tutin |first2=T. G. |last3=Warburg |first3=E. F. |date=1968 |publisher=Cambridge U.P |isbn=978-0-521-04656-5 |edition=2 |location=Cambridge, London}}</ref> (in the UK, between June and September<ref name=Readers>{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=250 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=978-0-276-00217-5}}</ref>) when white to pale pink, funnel-shaped flowers develop. Flowers are approximately {{cvt|1.9|–|2.5|cm}} across and are subtended by small bracts. The fruit are light brown, rounded and {{Cvt|3|–|4|mm}} wide. Each fruit contains 2 or 4 seeds that are eaten by birds and can remain viable in the soil for decades. The stems climb by twisting around other plant stems in a counter-clockwise direction.<ref name=Clapham1968/>
[[Image:Convolvulus arvenvis with mites.jpg|thumb|Flower with [[red velvet mite]]s]]

===Similar species===
''Convolvulus arvensis'' can be confused with a number of similar species. Key traits of ''C. arvensis'' are the small flowers often crowded together, and two sharp, backwards-pointed lobes at the base of the usually arrow-shaped leaf ending in a sharp apex.<ref name=Ontario>{{cite web |url=http://ontariowildflowers.com/main/species.php?id=202 |title=Field Bindweed (''Convolvulus arvensis'') |last=Muma |first=Walter |date= |website=Ontario Wildflowers |publisher=Walter Muma |access-date=10 July 2021}}</ref> Juvenile stems exude a milky sap when broken.<ref name=dreaded-bindweed>{{Cite web|url=https://extension.oregonstate.edu/news/bidding-farewell-dreaded-bindweed|title=Bidding Farewell to the Dreaded Bindweed|date=September 2008|website=Oregon State University Extension Service|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190716010715/https://extension.oregonstate.edu/news/bidding-farewell-dreaded-bindweed|archive-date=16 July 2019}}</ref> Similar species include:
*''[[Calystegia sepium]]'' - Large white flowers. Squarish<ref name=Ontario/> or rounded lobes at the base of the leaf.
*[[Calystegia spithamaea|''C. spithamaea'']] - Leaf apex is rounded. Large white flowers.<ref name=Ontario/> Only occurs in North America.
*''[[Fagopyrum tataricum]]'' - Annual.<ref name=dreaded-bindweed/> No milky sap.
*''[[Fallopia convolvulus]]'' - Small greenish flowers.<ref name=Ontario/> No milky sap.
*''[[Ipomoea]]'' spp. - Ornamental species are summer annuals.<ref name=dreaded-bindweed/> More rounded, heart-shaped leaves in most species.

In China, the most similar vining ''Convolvulus'' species is ''[[Convolvulus steppicola]]''. Most other ''Convolvulus'' species are [[shrub]]s or [[herbaceous]] perennials,<ref name=FOCkey>{{cite book |last1=Fang |first1=Ruizheng |last2=Staples |first2=George |date=1995 |chapter=''Convolvulus'' Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 1: 153. 1753 |chapter-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=107909 |title=Flora of China |url=http://www.efloras.org/volume_page.aspx?volume_id=2016&flora_id=2 |volume=16 (Gentianaceae through Boraginaceae) |location=St. Louis |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden Press |page= |isbn=}}</ref> however ''Convolvulus steppicola'' has a thick woody rootstock, almost no [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]], and only grows in northern [[Yunnan]],<ref name=FOCkey/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Fang |first1=Ruizheng |last2=Staples |first2=George |date=1995 |chapter=''Convolvulus steppicola'' Handel-Mazzetti, Symb. Sin. 7: 810. 1936 |chapter-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200018808 |title=Flora of China |url=http://www.efloras.org/volume_page.aspx?volume_id=2016&flora_id=2 |volume=16 (Gentianaceae through Boraginaceae) |location=St. Louis |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden Press |page= |isbn=}}</ref> where ''C. arvensis'' is absent.<ref name=FOC/>

==Ecology==
Plants are typically found inhabiting farmland,<ref name=FOC/><ref name=Readers/><ref name=Coombs2004>Coombs, E. M., et al., Eds. (2004). ''Biological Control of Invasive Plants in the United States.'' Corvallis: Oregon State University Press, 151.</ref> waste places,<ref name=FOC/><ref name=Readers/><ref name=Oberdorfer2001>{{cite book |last=Oberdorfer |first=Erich |date=2001 |title=Pflanzensoziologische Exkursionsflora für Deutschland und angrenzende Gebiete. Unter Mitarbeit von Angelika Schwabe und Theo Müller. 8., stark überarbeitete und ergänzte Auflage |location=Stuttgart (Hohenheim) |publisher=Eugen Ulmer |language=German |page=772 |isbn=3-8001-3131-5}}</ref> along roads,<ref name=FOC/><ref name=Coombs2004/><ref name=Oberdorfer2001/> in pastures,<ref name=Coombs2004/><ref name=Oberdorfer2001/> grassy slopes,<ref name=FOC/> and also along streams in North America.<ref name=Coombs2004/> It is able to colonise hot asphalt surfaces by covering it from the sides of roads, and worm its way between pavement stones.<ref name=Readers/> It grows from {{Convert|600 to 4500|m|ft}} in altitude in China, and is absent from the warmer southern provinces.<ref name=FOC/> It prefers dry areas with [[humus]]-poor, nutrient-rich and [[alkaline]] soils. It is a characteristic species in the [[Phytosociology|phytosociological]] vegetation [[Association (ecology)|association]] ''Convolvulo-Agropyretum'', belonging to the [[Elymus repens|couch grass]] [[dry grassland]]s alliance (called ''Convolvulo-Agropyrion repentis'' in syntaxonomy).<ref name=Oberdorfer2001/>

Like the other ''[[Convolvulus]]'' bindweeds of Eurasia, it is specifically pollinated by [[Halictidae|sweat bees]] in the genus ''[[Systropha]]''. These are specialists ([[Oligolecty|oligolectic]]) feeding upon the flowers of these plants, possessing unusual modifications of the [[Scopa (biology)|scopa]], such that almost the entire abdomen (including the dorsal surface) is used for carrying pollen, rather than the legs, as in most bees.<ref name="Michener">[[Charles D. Michener|Michener, C.D.]] (2000). ''The Bees of the World''. Johns Hopkins University Press</ref> Species of ''Systropha'' in central Europe (such as [[Systropha curvicornis|''S. curvicornis'']] and [[Systropha planidens|''S. planidens'']], both uncommon bees) are essentially entirely dependent upon ''C. arvensis''. Although both species specialise on the same plant species, ''S. curvicornis'' is a [[habitat]] generalist while ''S. planidens'' is only found in [[steppe]] habitats,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bogusch |first1=Petr |last2=Bláhová |first2=Eliška |last3=Horák |first3=Jakub |date=21 October 2020 |title=Pollen specialists are more endangered than non-specialised bees even though they collect pollen on flowers of non-endangered plants |journal=Arthropod-Plant Interactions |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=759–769 |doi=10.1007/s11829-020-09789-y|s2cid=226325867 }}</ref> although they are also found occurring together. The males of both species claim territories consisting of a patch of bindweed flowers, perching on the flowers in the afternoon after a regular patrol of their little patch for errant conspecific males, which, upon countenance, they proceed to attack the intruder by ramming him from the air with a specialised protuberance on their lower [[abdomen]]. 

Sometimes [[bumblebee]]s, honey bees or other insects are air-bombed, but never rammed. The males retreat inside the flower after the perching session, as it closes in the late afternoon, spending the night inside the flower and escaping at dawn before or after it fully closes (the females stay in underground tunnel nests). The males only land on flowers (sometimes of other plants), eschewing other perches, and feed on the [[nectar]]. Females forage for nectar and [[pollen]] in the morning and early afternoon while flowers stay open. Most copulation occurs in bindweed flowers: when a virgin female wanders into their patch, and the larger males find them busy at one of their flowers during morning patrol, the males pounce upon them without ado and immediately establish contact with their mutual genitalia, getting the job done on average 90 seconds later.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fraberger |first1=Raphaelo J. |last2=Ayasse |first2=Manfred |date=October 2007 |title=Mating Behavior, Male Territoriality and Chemical Communication in the European Spiral-Horned Bees, ''Systropha planidens'' and ''S. curvicornis'' (Hymenoptera: Halictidae) |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25086401 |journal=Journal of the Kansas Entomological Society |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=348–360 |doi= 10.2317/0022-8567(2007)80[348:MBMTAC]2.0.CO;2|jstor=25086401 |s2cid=86029808 |access-date=9 July 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These species are themselves specifically parasitised upon by the [[cuckoo bee]] ''[[Biastes brevicornis]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Müller |first1=Andreas |last2=Krebs |first2=Albert |last3=Amiet |first3=Felix |date=1997 |title=Bienen. Mitteleuropäische Gattungen, Lebensweise, Beobachtung |location=Augsburg |publisher=Naturbuch-Verlag |language=German |page= |isbn=3-89440-241-5}}</ref>

===As an invasive species===
[[File:Convolvulus (Convolvulus arvensis) - geograph.org.uk - 6502357.jpg|thumb|Growing in a disturbed area as weed]]
Outside its native range, field bindweed does not appear to be a significant threat to natural [[habitat]]s. It primarily requires [[disturbed ground]] (agricultural land),<ref name=Victoria1996>{{cite web |url=http://vro.agriculture.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/impact_bindweed |title=Impact Assessment - Bindweed (''Convolvulus arvensis'') in Victoria (Nox) |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=1996 |website=Victorian Resources Online |publisher=State of Victoria (Agriculture Victoria) |access-date=8 July 2021}}</ref><ref name=Zouhar2004>{{cite web |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/vine/conarv/all.html |title=SPECIES: ''Convolvulus arvensis'' |last=Zouhar |first=Kris |date=2004 |website=Fire Effects Information System |publisher=U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory |access-date=8 July 2021}}</ref> and is easily shaded out by taller shrubs and trees. It may dominate the ground flora in some low quality, open [[grassland]] areas, however.<ref name=Victoria1996/> In North America it can become the or a co-dominant plant in specific [[habitat]]s: the low vegetation found around vernal pools in Sacramento County, and around large pools in Tehama County, California; [[riparian corridor]]s in Wyoming and Colorado; aspen stands and mountain-mahogany (''[[Cercocarpus]]'' spp.) shrubland/grassland in Colorado; and disturbed riverbank areas in the [[Montreal]] area of Canada.<ref name=Zouhar2004/> 

In some nature parks, it is commonly found in areas of disturbed soil, such as camp grounds or around horse corrals in California. Similarly, the report of its invasive character from Colorado is from former agricultural land being restored to a more natural state by [[The Nature Conservancy]]. Employees for the same organisation also reported that it was a significant weed on an irrigated plot of farmland in northern Idaho where native bunchgrass and forbs were cultivated, insofar that it caused "decreasing biodiversity" on the land.<ref name=Zouhar2004/> 

A study conducted in 2003 has shown that with future global atmospheric carbon levels, field bindweed shows increased growth with increased atmospheric carbon which could potentially expand its range and outcompete native species that might not tolerate such conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ziska |first=L. H. |date=2003-01-02 |title=Evaluation of the growth response of six invasive species to past, present and future atmospheric carbon dioxide |url=https://academic.oup.com/jxb/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/jxb/erg027 |journal=Journal of Experimental Botany |language=en |volume=54 |issue=381 |pages=395–404 |doi=10.1093/jxb/erg027 |issn=0022-0957|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

It is thought to have little effect on native fauna, although it may sometime be eaten by farm livestock. It may cause [[Photosensitivity in animals|photosensitisation in susceptible animals]]. There is a report of its roots (rhizomes) being possibly poisonous to pigs.<ref name=Victoria1996/><ref name=Zouhar2004/> and the alkaloids it contains may be poisonous to horses in sufficient amounts.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Todd |first1=Fred G. |last2=Stermitz |first2=Frank R. |last3=Schultheis |first3=Partricia |last4=Knight |first4=Anthony P. |last5=Traub-Dargatz |first5=Josie |date=May 1995 |title=Tropane alkaloids and toxicity of ''Convolvulus arvensis'' |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=301–303 |doi=10.1016/0031-9422(94)00969-Z|pmid=7495531 }}</ref> There are also reports of it being eaten by sheep and pigs to control it without reported problems.<ref name=Zouhar2004/>

==Chemistry and uses==
Bindweed contains several [[alkaloid]]s which are toxic for mice, including [[pseudotropine]], and lesser amounts of [[tropine]], [[tropinone]], and [[cuscohygrine|meso-cuscohygrine]].<ref>Vet Hum Toxicol. 1995 Oct;37(5):452-4.  Toxicity of field bindweed (''Convolvulus arvensis'') to mice.  Schultheiss PC1, Knight AP, Traub-Dargatz JL, Todd FG, Stermitz FR.</ref> The alkaloids are also reported to give the plant [[psychoactive]] properties.
Its leaves contain [[glycosides]] and have been traditionally used to treat [[hypertension]] and as a [[laxative]] and [[diuretic]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sosnoskie |first=Lynn M. |last2=Hanson |first2=Bradley D. |last3=Steckel |first3=Lawrence E. |date=December 2020 |title=Field bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis): "all tied up" |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0890037X20000615/type/journal_article |journal=Weed Technology |language=en |volume=34 |issue=6 |pages=916–921 |doi=10.1017/wet.2020.61 |issn=0890-037X|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Economic impacts==
Although it produces attractive flowers, it is often unwelcome in gardens as a nuisance [[weed]] due to its rapid growth and choking of cultivated plants. It was most likely introduced into [[North America]] as a contaminant in crop seed as early as 1739, and became an [[invasive species]]. Its dense mats invade agricultural fields and reduce crop yields; it is estimated that crop losses due to this plant in the United States exceeded US$377 million in the year 1998 alone.<ref name=Coombs2004/> It is one of the most serious weeds of agricultural fields in many temperate regions of the US.<ref>{{cite web |title=The 10 Types of Weeds That Are Most Dangerous for Your Crops |url=https://www.gvcfarmsupply.com/the-10-types-of-weeds-that-are-most-dangerous-for-your-crops |website=www.gvcfarmsupply.com |access-date=6 June 2021 |language=en |date=2018-10-31}}</ref>

===Control and management===
Bindweed is difficult to eliminate. The roots may extend several metres deep.<ref name=dreaded-bindweed/><ref name=ControlBind>{{Cite web|url=https://extension.usu.edu/archive/tips-on-controlling-bindweed|title=Tips on Controlling Bindweed|last=Beddes|first=Taun|date=24 September 2014|website=Utah State University Extension|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190716010926/https://extension.usu.edu/archive/tips-on-controlling-bindweed|archive-date=16 July 2019}}</ref> New plants may sprout from seeds that are up to 20 years old.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.maine.gov/dacf/php/gotpests/weeds/factsheets/morning-glory-usda.pdf|title=Weed of the Week: Field Bindweed|last=USDA Forest Service|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190716011315/https://www.maine.gov/dacf/php/gotpests/weeds/factsheets/morning-glory-usda.pdf|archive-date=16 July 2019}}</ref> New plants can also form from root runners<ref name=ControlBind/> and root fragments.<ref name=dreaded-bindweed/>

Methods for controlling bindweed include:

* Physical removal: Bindweed can be controlled by pulling it out by hand or ploughing it up every three weeks, though this must continue for two to seven years to kill the plant entirely.<ref name=ControlBind/><ref name=Zouhar2004/><ref name=dreaded-bindweed/>
* Mulching: Applying a thick barrier to block sun may control bindweed.<ref name=ControlBind/>
* [[Soil solarisation]] for six to nine weeks in California was found to kill seedlings entirely, and control adult plants, but only for three weeks after treatment.<ref name=Zouhar2004/>
* Boiling water, placed on the plant, only practical for small areas.<ref>{{cite web |title=StackPath |url=https://www.gardeningknowhow.com/plant-problems/weeds/controlling-bindweed.htm |website=www.gardeningknowhow.com |access-date=6 June 2021}}</ref>
* Biological control: Some insects like the Field Bindweed moth (''Tyta luctuos'') and Bindweed gall mite (''Aceria malher'') can eat, distort or stunt bindweed, but do not fully control it.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/15101|title=''Convolvulus arvensis'' (bindweed)|last=Cortat|first=Ghislaine|date=15 November 2018|website=Invasive Species Compendium|publisher=CAB International|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190716035740/https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/15101|archive-date=16 July 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Exotic Plant Management Plan Environmental Assessment/Assessment of Effect February 2009 |url=https://parkplanning.nps.gov/showFile.cfm?sfid=68308&projectID=22569 |website=parkplanning.nps.gov |access-date=2025-11-28}}</ref>
* [[Grazing]]: In Minnesota, sheep are able to consistently completely rid an infested pasture of the bindweed in two seasons, but only when the pasture is used to grow annual grains.<ref name=Zouhar2004/>
* In general, plant species which grow vigorously in the winter and early spring are best at smothering emerging shoots.<ref name=Zouhar2004/>

==In culture==
In one of the tales collected by [[Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm]], ''Our Lady's Little Glass'', this flower is used by [[Mary, mother of Jesus]], to drink wine with when she helps free a wagoner's cart. The story goes on to say that "the little flower is still always called Our Lady's Little Glass".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.grimmstories.com/en/grimm_fairy-tales/our_ladys_little_glass |title=Our lady's little glass |author=<!--Not stated--> |date= |website=Grimms' Fairy Tales |access-date=12 July 2021}}</ref>
